conversation_lines.text: So can we lower it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried reducing it to 110 mg, but your home syringes are pre-filled for 120 mg and can’t be adjusted safely. So we’re keeping it the same for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s frustrating. I’m bleeding from my lungs and urine—could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very likely. You have a complex kidney cyst, and Lovenox could be contributing to the hematuria. You were supposed to see urology today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but I got admitted instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve rescheduled you. In the meantime, no flank pain or clots in urine, so nothing urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood clots? I still need the Lovenox forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Even though your Factor V Leiden test was negative, your history of multiple clots means you need lifelong anticoagulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate the injections twice a day. Is there another option?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discuss alternatives with hematology. They’ll help decide if a dose adjustment or different medication is safer for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your labs look stable—no infection, kidney function is okay, and no signs of internal bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the chest X-ray and belly X-ray?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No pneumonia, no bowel obstruction. Everything supports that this is an exacerbation of your chronic pain, not a new emergency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not crazy. It’s real, even if they can’t fix it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s very real. Chronic pain is complex. We’re not dismissing it—we’re managing it the best way we can right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re planning to discharge you today. Your pain is stable, and you’re eating and moving well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What changes should I expect?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue Lovenox at 120 mg twice daily for now. Start amitriptyline 25 mg at bedtime—take it regularly, not just when pain flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching to 5 mg tablets—take up to three every six hours as needed. Also, docusate and senna to prevent constipation from the pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with my PCP and surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and hematology for your Lovenox dose. Call if pain worsens or if you have heavy bleeding, shortness of breath, or chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel heard, at least.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We know this is tough. Keep taking your meds, rest, and we’ll get you more support through your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Follow up as scheduled, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of the hospitalists. You were brought in last night with chest pain and coughing up blood. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, the chest pain started yesterday while I was just sitting. It’s sharp, on both sides, worse when I breathe in. And I’ve been coughing up a little blood—same as before, about a teaspoon a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had this kind of pain with pulmonary embolisms before. Any shortness of breath, nausea, or sweating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. Just the pain and the coughing up blood. I’m worried it’s another clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We ran a CT scan with contrast, and it did show new blood clots in your lungs—specifically in the lower parts of both lungs. The good news is no heart strain or lung damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So it is another PE. But I’ve been on Lovenox. How did this happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good question. You have an IVC filter, and we know you’ve had clots on it before. Hematology thinks this may be due to not staying consistent with your Lovenox doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I try to take it, but sometimes I forget. And the syringes are hard to handle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adjusting your dose to 100 mg twice a day now because you’ve lost about 25 pounds recently. That makes the dosing more accurate and safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try to be more consistent. But the chest pain is bad. Can I get something for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on a heparin drip to prevent new clots. For pain, we’re giving oxycodone 5 mg every 4 hours as needed. We’re being cautious because of your history with narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but it really hurts. I’ve had this before—it feels just like a PE.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And that’s why we’re treating it. The oxycodone should help. We’re also checking for other causes of the bleeding. We ran ANCA tests to rule out autoimmune issues like Wegener’s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Autoimmune? I didn’t think of that. But it’s probably just from the clots, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. But since you’ve had long-term hemoptysis, we want to make sure there’s nothing else going on. The ANCA came back negative, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about my arm? It’s been swollen for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound. There’s a clot in the basilic vein in your left arm, from the elbow up. But the deep veins are fine. No DVT in your legs, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the arm clot isn’t dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a superficial clot, so lower risk. But we’ll keep monitoring. The main focus is your lungs and making sure you stay on anticoagulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my blood pressure meds—are they okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing your lisinopril, HCTZ, and amlodipine. Your BP has been well controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my cholesterol pill? I was on simvastatin 40 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reducing it to 20 mg daily. With amlodipine, higher doses increase the risk of muscle problems. Pharmacy recommended this change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, makes sense. I’ve been anxious too—can I keep taking my hydroxyzine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued it. Anxiety can make pain worse, so managing stress is part of your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your PTT levels are stabilizing—last one was 79.9, which is in the therapeutic range. That means the heparin is working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. How much longer will I be on the IV heparin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll transition you to the adjusted Lovenox dose today. Once we’re sure it’s holding steady, you can go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Home? That’d be great. But I’m scared I’ll miss a dose and get another clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s why we’re simplifying the dose and giving you pre-filled syringes. And please call your hematologist if you have any issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And my COPD meds—I’m still using the inhalers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep using the fluticasone-salmeterol twice daily and albuterol as needed. Your lungs sound clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. The acetaminophen upsets my stomach, though. Can I just stick with oxycodone for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re limiting oxycodone to 5 mg every 4 hours as needed. We avoid NSAIDs due to your allergies, so we’ll keep offering acetaminophen, but we’ll monitor your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re discharging you today. Your vitals are stable, and your labs are consistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take Lovenox 100 mg twice daily—no skipping. Use the oxycodone only for breakthrough pain. Keep taking your other meds as listed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow up with my PCP and hematologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Call them within a week. If you cough up more blood, have chest pain, or swelling, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and stay consistent with your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. You’re alert, breathing well, and your pain is controlled. All set to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll make sure to take the shots twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And keep using your inhaler. You’re doing the right thing for your health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. It’s been a lot, but this stay helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. Take it easy, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You were brought in last night with chest pain and right arm pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, the chest pain’s been getting worse, especially when I breathe in. And now my right bicep hurts—right where my old PICC line was. I’m worried it’s another clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Given your history of blood clots, that’s a valid concern. But let’s start with your breathing. Are you short of breath at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I can walk around, eat, garden like before. But the pain’s sharp when I inhale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds like pleuritic pain—common with pulmonary emboli. We did a chest X-ray early this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And? Did it show anything? A clot maybe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray didn’t show any new problems—no pneumonia, no fluid, no signs of a new large clot. Your lungs look stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve had clots before. Shouldn’t we do a CT scan to be sure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a fair question. But you’re already on Lovenox, and if there were a new clot, we’d keep you on the same treatment. So a CT wouldn’t change our plan right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess… but I just don’t want to ignore something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’re not ignoring it. We’re monitoring closely. We also did an ultrasound on your right arm because of the bicep pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And? Is there a clot there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the ultrasound showed normal blood flow. No deep vein thrombosis in your right arm. The tenderness might be from old scar tissue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. But the chest pain is still bad. Can I get something stronger for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You got morphine in the ER. We’ll start oxycodone 10mg every 4 hours as needed. It’s a bit stronger than your home dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was only taking 5mg at home. Is it safe to go up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for a short time. We’re watching closely because of your history. We’ll also keep acetaminophen available.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve been anxious too. Makes the pain feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We have hydroxyzine for anxiety, and you can take trazodone at night if you’re having trouble sleeping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Helps a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning again. I reviewed your labs from last night. Your white count was a bit high, but it’s coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that infection? Could that be causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but no fever or other signs. More likely inflammation from the clots or pain itself. Your troponin was normal—good for your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ve had chest pain for so long, I worry it’s my heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an EKG too. Shows sinus tachycardia—your heart’s racing a bit, probably from pain or anxiety. No heart attack signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain now? Better since the last dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little. Still sharp when I breathe deep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected with pleuritic pain. We’ll keep managing it. We also checked your blood pressure and COPD meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on Advair and albuterol. Still using the inhaler when I feel tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your oxygen levels are stable. No need for adjustments. We’ll keep your lisinopril, HCTZ, and amlodipine for blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the simvastatin? I remember they changed the dose last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, still 20mg. Pharmacy recommended that due to interaction risk with amlodipine. Lower dose, safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your repeat labs look better. White count dropped to 9.3, hemoglobin improved. Kidney function is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your pain seems more manageable. We might try lowering the oxycodone back toward your home dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to jump back into severe pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. Maybe try 7.5mg for a dose and see how you do. We’re also focusing on non-medication strategies—breathing, relaxation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doc, I’ve been thinking. I know I messed up before with my meds. But I’ve been taking Lovenox every 12 hours, I swear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you. And that’s important. You’ve had recurrent clots, but no new signs this time. Your IVC filter helps too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just hate living in fear of the next one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We’ll keep you on Lovenox and schedule follow-up with your hematologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your EKG today shows sinus rhythm. Heart rate slowed down. Less strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. And the chest pain? I think it’s better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re moving easier, breathing deeper. We’ll keep oxycodone 10mg for now, but plan to taper soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking at discharge tomorrow morning. How do you feel about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ready to go home, but nervous about the pain coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with oxycodone 10mg every 4 hours for three days, then back to 5mg as needed. That should cover the transition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain management appointment is next week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, on ___ . They’ll help fine-tune your plan. Keep using acetaminophen, hydroxyzine for anxiety, and your COPD meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Pain’s improved, labs are stable, and you’re walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. Thank you for listening. I was really scared it was another big clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But we checked everything we could safely. No new clots, no DVT, no heart issue. You’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I keep the Lovenox the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 100mg every 12 hours. Don’t skip doses. Call your doctor if you have bleeding, severe pain, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the oxycodone—only for a few days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Two pills every 4 hours for three days, then one. Stop when you can manage with acetaminophen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try the breathing and relaxation stuff too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the spirit. And keep your follow-up appointments. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in clinic if needed, but I expect you’ll keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of the hospitalists. I understand you've been having chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, the chest pain started a couple days ago. It’s in the lower left side, same spot as my last pulmonary embolism. Hurts worse when I breathe or press on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds like pleuritic pain. Any shortness of breath, cough, or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had some shortness of breath and a cough. I always have a little blood in my sputum—hemoptysis—but it hasn’t changed. And I’ve had chills and low-grade fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the abdominal pain and diarrhea—when did those start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Diarrhea started about three days ago—yellowish, loose stools, four times a day. No blood. Then the next day, I got pain in the lower left abdomen. Feels like when I had diverticulitis before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And have you been taking your Lovenox regularly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I ran out five days ago. I called my PCP, but got voicemail. I couldn’t get a refill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Being off anticoagulation could explain some of this. We’ve ordered a CT scan to check for clots. We’ll also run blood tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. Good news—no pulmonary embolism. But we did see something concerning: a new blood clot near your IVC filter. It’s not blocking flow, but it’s new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? Could it move?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The filter caught it, which is exactly what it’s supposed to do. There’s no sign it’s causing damage or leaking. Vascular surgery reviewed it and said no surgery is needed. But it likely formed because you were off Lovenox.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I just restart the Lovenox?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve already restarted it. You’ll need to stay on it indefinitely. We’re also sending a prescription to your pharmacy for a month’s supply.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the chest pain? Is it from the clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain isn’t from a new PE. Your heart tests are normal—no heart attack. The pain is likely musculoskeletal, maybe costochondritis. It’s reproducible when I press here, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, that’s exactly where it hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That supports it being a chest wall issue. We’ll manage it with acetaminophen and a short course of oxycodone if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have something now? It’s been really bothering me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I can give you 5 mg of oxycodone now. But we need to be careful—your history includes substance use, and we want to avoid over-reliance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but the pain is real. I’m not trying to misuse anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you. We’ll treat your pain appropriately. We’re also giving hydroxyzine for anxiety, which can make pain worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain now, about two hours after the medication?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, but still there. Can I have another dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet—it’s only been two hours. The oxycodone is every four hours as needed. Let’s try breathing exercises and repositioning. We can reassess in two hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I had an accident—fecal incontinence earlier. I’m embarrassed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay, Mr. ___. It happens, especially with diarrhea. We’ve noted it. Your stools are softening, which is a good sign. The diarrhea seems mild—likely viral. No antibiotics needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want this to stop. And I’m worried about the clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The clot is stable. The filter did its job. The key is staying on Lovenox. We’re setting you up with your PCP to manage refills so this doesn’t happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable—kidneys, liver, and electrolytes are fine. No signs of infection. We’re planning to discharge you today if you’re feeling okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? What about the IVC filter? Shouldn’t someone check it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vascular surgery reviewed it. The filter shifted slightly but isn’t piercing the vein. No intervention needed. But you must follow up with your doctor to monitor it long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve missed a few appointments. I’ll try to do better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve already called your pharmacy—your Lovenox is ready. We’re also faxing your PCP with the details. You need to see them within a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about pain meds when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with 20 tablets of oxycodone 5 mg—take one every six hours only if needed. Don’t exceed that. Continue acetaminophen as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my anxiety? I still can’t sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking trazodone and hydroxyzine at night. Avoid screens before bed. If it continues, talk to your PCP about adjusting the dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home. Remember: take Lovenox every day, follow up with your PCP, and keep your pain clinic appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll do my best to stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Call if you have chest pain that worsens, shortness of breath, or any bleeding. Otherwise, take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge—how are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Chest pain is better, stomach feels calmer. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one last thing—should I worry about the kidney cyst they saw on the scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s been there and is stable. They recommend an MRI in a few months to check it. Mention it at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I will. Thanks for answering all my questions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Stay safe, and take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—everything looks good. You’re officially discharged. Go home, rest, and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the help. I’ll stay on my meds and make that appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were admitted this morning for chest pain. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, thanks. I’ve had this sharp chest pain when I breathe in. It feels just like when I had that pulmonary embolism before. It’s on the left side and gets worse when I take a deep breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s called pleuritic chest pain. Given your history of blood clots and being on Lovenox, we take this very seriously. You said you’ve been keeping up with your injections?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I only missed one dose this week. I know how important it is. I even have extra boxes at home—I’ve been using those after my last refill ran out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your pharmacy record shows your last prescription ended recently, so we’ll make sure you leave with enough Lovenox this time. We’ve restarted your 120 mg twice daily here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I don’t want another clot. My mom and uncle both died from blood clots, so I know it’s serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That family history is definitely concerning. We’re watching you closely. We’ve done blood tests, an EKG, and a chest X-ray to rule out a heart attack or pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And? Is it another PE?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oxygen levels are good, and your heart enzymes are normal—no sign of a heart attack. The EKG didn’t show strain on the right side of your heart, which we’d expect with a large PE.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no PE? But the pain feels the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We didn’t do another CT scan because your vital signs are stable and we wouldn’t change treatment anyway. You’re already on full anticoagulation. If there’s a small PE, it’s being treated with your current Lovenox dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. That makes sense. What about that filter in my vein? Could it have moved?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great question. We did an X-ray of your abdomen, and the IVC filter is still in place—stable at the L2-3 level. No signs of migration or complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been worried about that. I also noticed some swelling in my left foot. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your legs—no tenderness, warmth, or difference in size. So it’s unlikely to be a new DVT. The swelling might be from something else, like mild fluid retention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve also been coughing up a little blood sometimes. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, hemoptysis is something we monitor. You’ve had tracheomalacia—weakness in the airway—which can cause irritation and blood-tinged sputum, especially on anticoagulants.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a new lung bleed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of that. Your chest X-ray is clear, and your hemoglobin is stable. Pulmonology reviewed your case and agrees it’s likely related to your airway condition and anticoagulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also peeing blood sometimes. That’s been going on for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your urine showed red blood cells, but no infection. Since it’s chronic and you have no pain or clots, we’re not concerned about an acute issue. We’ll follow up with your primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’ve been anxious about all this. Can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We have hydroxyzine for anxiety, and we’ll also give you a small supply of lorazepam to use at home if needed—just four tablets, since we want to be careful with sedatives.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. My chest pain is still bothering me. Can I take more pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you IV dilaudid in the ER, and you’re on your regular oxycodone. We’ll keep that going. We’re sending you home with 20 tablets of 5 mg oxycodone to take every four hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had chronic pain from my hernias and past clots. It’s hard to manage sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re continuing all your usual medications, including your inhalers for COPD and your blood pressure and cholesterol pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been smoking, though. I know I shouldn’t.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tobacco use increases your clotting risk and worsens lung disease. We strongly encourage quitting. We can connect you with resources if you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe later. Right now, I just want to get better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. I wanted to update you. Your repeat labs show your white count was a bit high last night—12.2—but it’s improving today, and there’s no sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the pain or stress?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your blood cultures and urine culture came back negative. The urine had mixed flora, but that’s likely contamination from the skin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. We’re confident this isn’t an infection. Your pain is most likely related to your history of pulmonary embolism and pleuritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today. Your condition is stable, and you’re breathing comfortably on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your Lovenox 120 mg twice daily. Don’t let it run out—call your doctor before the supply ends. Also, take your other meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Please call hematology to schedule an appointment—they can evaluate your clotting disorder. Also, see your primary care doctor within a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve missed those before, but I’ll try this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s been hard, but it’s important. We’re also sending you with stool softeners—docusate and senna—since oxycodone can cause constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have the nurse go over your discharge instructions and medications. You should be ready to leave by noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick final check before you go. How’s your pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I think I can manage at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember—Lovenox twice daily, no skipping. Call hematology, stay on your meds, and reach out if chest pain worsens or you have trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. Stay safe and keep in touch with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of the hospitalists. I see you came in with chest pain, fever, and abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had this sharp chest pain for about a day and a half—worse when I breathe. I also had a fever up to 102, chills, and left-sided belly pain. I’ve been coughing a little and even spit up a bit of blood, but it’s not more than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve had similar chest pain before with blood clots. Are you still on your Lovenox injections?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been taking it twice a day like I’m supposed to. I haven’t missed any doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. You mentioned your stepmother had pneumonia—did you spend time with her recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I was at her house last week. I started a Z-pack two days ago—only taken two pills so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of asplenia and the fever, we’re concerned about infection. We’re going to start you on antibiotics—vancomycin, metronidazole, and levofloxacin—to cover possible abdominal or lung infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that interact with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve checked—no major interactions. We’ll monitor you closely. We also got a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis to look for any source of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the chest pain? Could it be another clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The outside hospital did a CT angiogram, and it didn’t show a pulmonary embolism. Your troponins are normal, and your EKG doesn’t suggest heart strain. So it’s unlikely to be a new clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve had this pain before with clots. It feels the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But you’re on therapeutic Lovenox, and the scan was clear. We think this episode is more likely related to your chronic pain or possibly irritation from coughing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… what about the blood I coughed up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned it was about a teaspoon—very small. Given your anticoagulation and chronic lung issues, this can happen occasionally and isn’t alarming unless it increases.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I just worry because of my history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. We’re taking your symptoms seriously. We’ll keep monitoring you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. I’ve reviewed your CT scan results. There’s no sign of infection, diverticulitis, or other acute issues in your abdomen. The IVC filter is stable, with a small non-blocking clot above it—same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous—the clot near the filter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not blocking blood flow, and it’s been stable on prior scans. As long as you stay on Lovenox, we don’t expect it to grow. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. What about the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue them for now since you had a fever and we wanted to cover all bases. But with no source found, we may stop them tomorrow if you keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs came back. White count is slightly elevated at 11.2, but no left shift—so likely not a serious infection. More likely due to stress or inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why the fever then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be viral—especially since you were exposed to pneumonia. Or it could be related to your chronic inflammation. Your lactate is normal, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling better. The fever’s gone, and the belly pain is much less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. You’re tolerating food well, and your bowel movements are back to normal. We’ll likely discontinue the antibiotics later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still mild, I see. We’ll continue your usual pain meds as needed—oxycodone. But we’re watching closely to avoid overuse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we noticed a small 4mm nodule in your lung on prior imaging. It hasn’t changed. But you’ll need a follow-up CT in six months to monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s too small to tell, but most nodules like this are benign. The key is to watch for any growth over time. Your primary doctor can schedule the next scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been meaning to ask—can we switch from lorazepam for sleep? I’m worried about dependence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve started you on trazodone at night. It’s safer for long-term use and helps reduce reliance on benzodiazepines like lorazepam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I want to do things the right way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you in the morning. Your symptoms have resolved, and all tests are reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to come back for anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—follow up with your primary care doctor and hematology. They’ll help manage your anticoagulation and monitor the lung nodule and kidney cyst.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I’ve missed some appointments before… but I’ll try to go this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. Staying on top of your care helps prevent complications. We’re sending the records to your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your discharge is approved. You’re off antibiotics, pain is controlled, and you’re back to your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Continue all your home medications, especially Lovenox. Watch for increasing chest pain, shortness of breath, or more hemoptysis—and seek care if they occur.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the kidney cyst they mentioned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s stable but slightly changed. Your PCP will arrange an MRI when needed. No action now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and please keep those follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’ve received your discharge instructions and prescriptions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, everything’s in order.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re cleared to go home. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, chest pain again. Same as last time. And I’ve got this pain in my right side when I sit up. I need something for the pain—2 mg of Dilaudid IV and 2 mg Ativan to sleep, like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you’re in pain. We’ll manage that, but first I need to understand what’s going on. You’ve been on Lovenox for your blood clots—have you been taking it regularly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice a day. I haven’t missed a dose. But I keep getting these clots. What’s wrong with me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan tonight, and it showed a small clot in your aorta, near where you’ve had clots before. It’s in the distal aortic arch, just after the left subclavian artery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another clot? But I’m on Lovenox! How is that possible?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we’re trying to figure out. You’ve had recurrent clots despite being on anticoagulants. Vascular surgery looked at the images and said the clot is in a tricky spot—too risky to remove surgically.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now? Just keep taking shots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. Hematology recommended starting a heparin drip tonight to make sure your blood is thin enough. We also ordered a test called anti-Xa to check if your Lovenox levels are therapeutic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help with the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The heparin won’t help the pain directly, but treating the clot should help over time. We’ll give you your usual oxycodone for pain, 10 mg every 4 hours as needed. No IV narcotics tonight, but we can adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine. But I need to sleep. Can I have the Ativan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll order 1 mg of lorazepam at bedtime for you. We’ll monitor your breathing, especially with your COPD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning look stable. Your white count is normal, and your troponin is negative—so no heart attack. The anti-Xa level from yesterday was low, but it was drawn too soon after your Lovenox dose, so it might not reflect your true level.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So was the Lovenox not working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t think so. We redrew the anti-Xa today, timed correctly, and we’ll get the result later. But your history shows you’ve had clots even when on therapy, so we suspect you may have an underlying hypercoagulable state.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what? My mom and uncle both died from clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Family history increases your risk. You’ve tested negative for Factor V Leiden and anticardiolipin antibodies before, but we may need more testing. Hematology will help with that after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the plan today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on the heparin drip for now. Once we confirm your Lovenox is working, we’ll switch back. We also want to start you on aspirin to help prevent further clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Aspirin? I thought that was for heart attacks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It helps with arterial clots like this one. It works differently than Lovenox. Together, they give better protection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your repeat anti-Xa level came back therapeutic. That means your Lovenox is working at the right level.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why did I get another clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. It could be that the spot in your aorta is prone to clotting—maybe from old injury or a small abnormality. Since you’ve had clots there before, it might be a weak point.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With continued anticoagulation, it should shrink. Vascular surgery wants a repeat CT scan in one month to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the aspirin—you said start it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start 325 mg daily. Also, your simvastatin dose is being increased to 40 mg to help with clotting risk and cholesterol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today? Any chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still some ache under my left armpit, but not sharp. Cough’s a bit better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your repeat labs are stable. No signs of infection or anemia. The heparin drip is being stopped, and you’re back on your regular Lovenox injections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m going home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow morning. We just want to make sure you’re stable on your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need close follow-up with hematology to look into why you keep forming clots. Also, vascular surgery wants that CT scan in a month. And your primary doctor should check the kidney spot we saw.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Kidney spot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a small area in your left kidney. It’s not new, and it’s gotten smaller, but we recommend an ultrasound to make sure it’s benign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. You’ll continue your Lovenox, add aspirin, and take simvastatin 40 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, oxycodone 10 mg every 4 hours as needed. But please follow up with pain management. They can help with long-term strategies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want the pain gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But we also need to make sure your treatment is safe and effective long-term. The hematology visit is key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’ll try to make the appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please do. And call if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, or any new symptoms. Otherwise, see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.text: And my leg? I was worried about the IVC filter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why the groin pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be muscular. You mentioned tightness. No swelling, pulses are strong, and strength is normal. We think it could be a muscle spasm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had clots before. I don’t want to miss something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand your concern. That’s why we did the scans. We’re also seeing improvement in the old aortic arch clot compared to your last scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it suggests your anticoagulation is working. We’ll keep you on enoxaparin here and continue your home dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there. Chest hurts when I move or breathe out. Leg feels a bit better, but I’m stiff.

conversation_lines.text: Your vitals are stable. Blood pressure is 146/99, which is acceptable. We’ll keep monitoring. We’re not seeing signs of infection or heart strain.

conversation_lines.text: I’ve been in bed most of the time. I just don’t feel like moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s hard, but gentle movement helps prevent complications. We’ll encourage you to walk a bit later if you’re able.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your labs. Everything looks stable—white count normal, no electrolyte issues. Your kidney function is good.

conversation_lines.text: Any idea about the chest pain? Could it be the hernia?
