conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But it’s not new. Why now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes old conditions flare up. With your recent illness and coughing, it might have been aggravated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had the flu two weeks ago. Coughed a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could definitely contribute. We’ll manage your pain with oxycodone as prescribed by your PCP and keep an eye on your mobility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit better. I walked to the bathroom without too much pain. Chest still hurts when I take a deep breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your oxygen levels are good, and lungs are clear. We’ll keep supporting your breathing with your inhalers as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. We’ve ruled out dangerous causes. The plan is to continue your current meds and prepare for discharge tomorrow if you keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m frustrated. I wish we knew exactly what’s causing the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Sometimes, especially with complex histories like yours, we can’t pinpoint a single cause. But we’ve ruled out life-threatening issues, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home today. Your pain has improved, and you’re walking well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with your PCP for pain management and see Dr. ___ in hematology to discuss your clotting disorder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will my meds change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No changes. Continue enoxaparin twice daily, aspirin, simvastatin, and oxycodone as needed for pain. Same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your oxycodone as prescribed. If it gets worse or you develop shortness of breath, fever, or swelling, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having chest pain and trouble breathing. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had this bad cough since I finished my last prednisone. It’s so bad it makes my ribs and chest ache. And I can’t catch my breath like normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were recently treated for influenza and bronchitis, and you have COPD. Did you stop your medications early or do anything physically demanding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did finish the prednisone, but then I helped my cousin shovel snow. I know I shouldn’t have, but I felt okay at the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could definitely make things worse. Your CT scan showed something we need to monitor — a clot in the aortic arch. But the good news is it hasn’t changed from your last scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A clot? Is that dangerous? I’ve had blood clots before — my mom and uncle both died from them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand your concern. Given your history — factor V Leiden and prior clots — you're at higher risk. But the vascular team reviewed your case and said no immediate surgery or intervention is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. But the chest pain is sharp, especially when I cough. Can I get something stronger for pain? I usually take oxycodone, but I was hoping for IV Dilaudid like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted the pain team. They don’t think IV narcotics are necessary right now. Your oxygen levels are stable, and your pain can be managed with oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m really uncomfortable. Can I at least get one dose of IV Dilaudid? After that, I’ll go back to my regular oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: After discussing it, we agreed to give you one dose of IV Dilaudid to help you through the worst of it. But we’ll switch back to your oral oxycodone after that, as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just want to feel better. What about my breathing? I still wheeze a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lungs have wheezes and some rhonchi, but no infection on imaging. We’re continuing your DuoNeb treatments every four hours while you're awake. You’ll take them at home until your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve been stable overnight — heart rate and oxygen levels are good. Your blood work shows a high white count, but that’s likely from the steroids, not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m okay to go home? What about the clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can go home today. The aortic clot is stable. You need to keep your CT scan appointment at 1:30 today and see Dr. Patel at 2 PM. Continue your enoxaparin — no breaks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the prednisone? I just started a new taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, finish the full taper as prescribed. Also complete your Levaquin antibiotic. And remember — no driving or alcohol while on narcotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow everything. Thanks for explaining it clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call your doctor if you have worsening pain, shortness of breath, or any concerns before your appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’ll make sure to get that scan done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll update your primary doctor about this stay. You’re cleared to discharge when you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. I’ll try to take it easy this time — no shoveling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good plan. Rest and recovery are key, especially with your lung and clotting history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll stop smoking too. I know it’s not helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s one of the best things you can do for your lungs and circulation. I’m glad to hear that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I think I’m ready to head out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take these discharge instructions with you. You’re doing well — just keep up with your care plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Patel. I understand you’ve been having swelling in your legs and trouble breathing. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, my right leg started swelling two nights ago. I went to the ER but left because I didn’t want to wait. Came back the next day—now both legs are swollen. And I can’t catch my breath when I walk or even just sitting sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve been on Lovenox for your history of clots—have you missed any doses?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’ve been taking it every day like I’m supposed to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. You also mentioned chest pain and coughing. Is the chest pain worse with breathing or movement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s mostly when I cough. Hurts right here in the middle. But I don’t think it’s my heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That helps. We’ll check things out. I’m going to listen to your lungs and heart now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear wheezing in your lungs, but your heart sounds are regular. Your legs have pitting edema up to the knees. We’ll run some tests to see what’s causing this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it another clot? I’ve had those before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking for that. You had an ultrasound on your right leg earlier today—good news, no new clot there. We’ll do more imaging to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your CT scan. No pulmonary embolism. Your lungs look clear—no pneumonia or fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why am I so short of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Part of it is your COPD. We’re giving you albuterol treatments every few hours to open your airways. That should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my legs? They’re killing me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned this might be heart-related swelling. Your BNP level is elevated, which suggests your heart isn’t pumping as efficiently as it should—called heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Heart failure? But I’m not that old.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not just about age. You have high blood pressure, COPD, and a history of clots—all of which strain the heart over time. We’ll start a diuretic to help your body get rid of the extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s a water pill?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Torsemide. It’ll help reduce the swelling and make breathing easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning show your white count is coming down, which is good. The infection marker was a bit high yesterday, but no fever now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Doesn’t look like it. Your troponin was normal—so no heart attack. The chest pain seems to be from coughing, not your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the heart ultrasound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The echo was hard to read because of your breathing, but we could see your heart’s squeezing okay—EF over 55%. We couldn’t see the atrial myxoma clearly, so you may need a better echo later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that myxoma for years. It hasn’t caused problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still, we want to keep an eye on it. For now, we’re focusing on your breathing and swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your leg swelling is already improving. The diuretic is working. Edema is now only mild, down to your lower legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, they feel a lot better. I’m peeing more, too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we want. We also noticed you’ve been drinking about five cans of V8 juice a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s got vitamins. Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s high in sodium—about 2 grams a day just from that. With heart issues, too much salt makes your body hold onto fluid. Try to cut back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. I didn’t know. I’ll stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, the high-dose prednisone you’ve been on for COPD can cause fluid retention too. We’ll help you taper that safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing has improved. You’re not needing albuterol as often, and your oxygen levels are stable on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I feel better. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting close. We want to make sure your fluid levels are stable and your pain is controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still have chest pain when I cough. Can I get something stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve kept your oxycodone available for breakthrough pain. Since you’re allergic to morphine and others, we’ll stick with that. But we’ll also encourage non-opioid options long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on it for years. It’s the only thing that works.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But we want to make sure you’re safe and not over-relying on it. We’ll work with you on a plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs today look much better. Your electrolytes are stable, and kidney function is normal. We’re confident you’re ready for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Where will I go? I’ve been living in my car.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Social work has been trying to connect you with shelters, but I understand you’ve declined. We still want to make sure you have support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to get back to my routine. I’ll be okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled a follow-up with a clinic that accepts your insurance. It’s important to see someone to manage your medications and check your heart and lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. But I don’t like doctors’ offices.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re officially ready to go home. Your breathing is much better, legs are nearly back to normal, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. What meds am I taking now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue Lovenox twice daily for your clot risk. Torsemide once daily for fluid. Your inhalers—albuterol for breathing, Spiriva daily, and Advair twice a day. And oxycodone as needed for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood pressure pill?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We stopped the amlodipine because your blood pressure has been in the 100s to 120s. We’ll let your follow-up doctor decide if you need it again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And if my legs swell again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Watch your salt, stay on your meds, and come in if swelling returns or gets worse. Same if breathing gets harder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us. And please keep that follow-up appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Ready to get out of here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re alert, breathing well, and walking independently. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy. Stay out of the cold, keep using your inhalers, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—we’re sending you home with instructions and your follow-up details. Please read them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we can ask. You’ve made great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Feels good to breathe again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. You’re discharged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been having a lot of trouble breathing, especially when I walk. It’s been getting worse over the last couple months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had several hospital visits recently for similar issues. Were you on prednisone during that time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been on steroids for weeks now. But it hasn’t helped. I still can’t catch my breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We also noticed you have a history of COPD and blood clots. Did you have any leg swelling this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. My legs are okay. But I do have chest tightness sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We ran a CT scan of your chest to check for clots or pneumonia. Good news—it didn’t show a pulmonary embolism.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a clot? Then why can’t I breathe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s something new—we found a narrowing in your left pulmonary artery. It wasn’t there a few months ago. We’re not sure yet if it’s causing your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? Do I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. The pulmonology team reviewed it and said it doesn’t need urgent treatment. They’ll follow up with you later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… but I still need help with my breathing. And I want to make sure I get my oxycodone. My back pain is killing me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand the pain. But we need to be careful with opioids, especially since you're on other medications and have a history of multiple prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not abusing them. I just need relief. My doctor in ___ gives them to me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your records. You’ve seen over 30 different providers in the past year for pain. That raises concerns about safety and coordination of care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I go where I can get help. No one else listens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hear you. But combining opioids with other sedatives can be risky. We’re not going to prescribe them unless there’s a clear medical need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what am I supposed to do about the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll focus on non-opioid options and work with your primary care team. Long-term, a consistent provider can help manage this better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did a chest X-ray yesterday—your lungs look clear. Today, you’ll have a VQ scan to check for chronic clots in the lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another test? What’s it for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Since you’ve had multiple clots before, we want to see if old clots might be affecting your breathing. The VQ scan compares airflow and blood flow in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s painless. Just some breathing exercises and a small IV injection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The VQ scan showed a mismatch in the left lower lung. It could be from old clots, but it’s not an emergency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is that why I can’t breathe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but it doesn’t explain everything. You’re not low on oxygen, and your heart function is normal. We also did a stress test—no signs of heart disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had one of those a month ago too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that. It’s good both were normal. But it makes us think your symptoms might be more complex than just lung or heart issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I heard you coughed up a little blood last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, just a little. I was coughing hard. Maybe it’s from that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The nurse mentioned the blood might have come from your IV line. But we did another X-ray, and there’s a new shadow in your right lung.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be. Or atelectasis—collapsed air sacs from not breathing deeply. We’ll watch it. No antibiotics yet unless it gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. White count was high when you came in, but it’s coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was I infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection. The high count might be from steroids or stress. Your liver scan showed fatty liver, but that’s not related to this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed everything—CT, VQ, stress test, labs. No acute illness found. Your breathing pattern changes when we listen, which makes us think behavior might be playing a role.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not faking this. I feel terrible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe you’re suffering. But sometimes stress and anxiety can worsen breathing. And with your history of frequent hospital visits, we want to make sure you get the right long-term support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to feel better. I’m tired of being sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. Your breathing is stable, and no new issues came up overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I still feel short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s at your baseline. We can’t find a treatable cause. We’ll keep your COPD meds the same, but we’re increasing your Advair dose to help control inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Lovenox? I’m scared of clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You must keep taking Lovenox. You’re at high risk for clots. Please don’t stop it, even if you feel like giving up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t know… I just don’t care anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear that. It’s been a long road. But you’re not alone. We’re setting up follow-up with pulmonology. And please talk to someone about how you’re feeling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your discharge meds. We’re keeping everything the same except Advair, which is now a higher strength. No opioids this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not unless there’s a clear reason. We’re concerned about the risks, especially with your history. Please talk to your primary doctor about safer pain options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine. But I hope someone actually helps me next time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re trying to help by making sure you’re safe. Please keep your follow-up appointments. Your health depends on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. A friend is picking you up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, he’s coming soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember: take your Lovenox, use your inhalers, and call if you cough up more blood or can’t breathe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pulmonology will call you this week. And please think about talking to someone about the stress you’re under.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.text: Will I need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but you’re stable. It might be from dehydration or frequent albuterol use. We’re giving you fluids to see if it improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your lactate is still high. We’re going to do a CT scan today to look at your heart and lungs more closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it show if the myxoma is worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll look for that. But we also need to check for blood clots, pneumonia, or other causes of your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your CT results. There’s a mass in your right atrium — about 1.9x2.4 cm. It could be a clot or a tumor. It’s not in the typical spot for a myxoma.

conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a myxoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I told you, I try. But I lose track sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. The clot appears stable compared to past scans. Surgery isn’t needed unless it causes problems. We’ll continue your Lovenox.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the cancer they said I might have?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT showed a 1.5 cm lesion in your right kidney. It could be a cyst or a small cancer. We’ll need an MRI to know more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can’t I get the MRI now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned claustrophobia. We tried an ultrasound, but it wasn’t clear. MRI is the next step, but it’s not available inpatient. You’ll need it as an outpatient in about six months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Six months? What if it’s cancer and it spreads?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lesions this small don’t need immediate treatment. If it were over 4 cm, we’d act fast. At 1.5 cm, watchful waiting is standard. We’ll make sure you get the follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re placing a PICC line so we can give you IV fluids and draw blood easily during your stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll numb the area first. You might feel pressure, but not sharp pain. It’s a quick procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your back pain — you said you dropped a heavy toolbox?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, last week. Felt something pop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT shows a mild compression fracture at L2. It’s likely from that injury. It should heal with rest and pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I get something stronger for the pain? Tylenol upsets my stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re cautious with opioids because of your history. But given the fracture, we’ll give low-dose oxycodone for a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried the kidney ultrasound, but the images weren’t clear. MRI is still the best next step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate the idea of waiting. What if it’s bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand your worry. But small kidney lesions like yours are common and usually slow-growing. Immediate action isn’t needed. We’ll help you schedule the MRI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lactate is down to 2.5 after fluids. That’s a good sign. Your kidney function also improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the dehydration was causing that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Albuterol can also contribute. You’re on high doses, which may explain some of your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We spoke with cardiology. The mass in your heart is likely a clot, not a myxoma. Cardiac MRI confirmed it’s not cancerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s a clot? But I’m on Lovenox.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we think you may not be taking it consistently. The clot hasn’t grown, so we’ll keep you on it and check with an echo in a few months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to keep getting hospitalized like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work on a plan. Staying on your meds and having stable housing would help a lot. Social work can help connect you to resources.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t trust the system. I feel like I’m just bounced around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. But your health depends on consistent care. We can help you find a primary doctor who knows your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is better. You’re walking without desatting. We’re planning to discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you 8 pills of 5mg oxycodone — enough for two days. After that, try acetaminophen with a stomach protector.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. But what if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the lidocaine patch and heating pad. If it’s unbearable, go to urgent care. But avoid ER unless necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the kidney MRI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send the order. You’ll get a call to schedule it in about six months. It’s important — please don’t skip it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. But I don’t have a phone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a written reminder and contact info. You can check in at the clinic if you’re nearby.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the heart clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on Lovenox. No changes. We’ll repeat an echo in a few months to check if it’s shrinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Vital signs are stable. We’re ready to discharge you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m scared to go back to living in my car.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given your info to social work. They’ll reach out to help with housing resources. Please follow up with your doctor in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. I just want to feel better and not keep coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We want that too. Keep taking your meds, go to your appointments, and reach out if you’re struggling. You’re not alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I’ll do better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll support you. Here’s your discharge paperwork. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — if you feel chest pain or shortness of breath gets worse, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just stay on track. You’ve made progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy on that back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep using the heating pad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, you’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.
